title: Dedication
hook: the good of five years given away to all beings
tomorrow: the teacher is dying. who teaches after him?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four immeasurables: kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity, sent out with no edge. Immeasurable. Today, what happens to the good those practices make.

After a big win, some players point up at the stands: that one was for my grandmother. Buddhists have an older version. The commentary on a short text, the Tirokudda Sutta, tells it. King Bimbisara gave the Buddha and his monks a meal, and that night he heard wailing around the palace: relatives of his who had died, waiting outside the walls, hoping for a share. The next day he gave again, and this time he dedicated the gift to them. The sutta's own words are simple: may this be for our relatives; may our relatives be happy. So can you give away the good you've done?
screen: `THAT ONE WAS FOR GRANDMA.` → `A KING GIVES A MEAL.` → `WAILING OUTSIDE THE WALLS.` → `MAY THIS BE FOR OUR RELATIVES.`

segments.voice: Buddhists say yes, and they disagree, warmly, about how. Here are the two voices. The first starts from the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's words: "Purity and impurity belong to oneself, no one can purify another." Karma isn't money, this side says; it can't be wired into someone else's account. So what does a dedication do? It invites. When the departed, or anyone, learns of the good deed and rejoices in it, that gladness is a good act of their own. In Pali the rejoicing is anumodana, and in Theravada temples you may hear people say sadhu, sadhu, well done, when a gift is offered. The second voice, strong in the Mahayana, says: giving the good away is generosity too, and generosity grows the good instead of spending it. Shantideva ends his guide to the bodhisattva's way with a whole chapter of dedication, giving the good he has made to the sick, the frightened, beings in every kind of pain. And at Mai's family's chùa, as in other Mahayana temples, the chanting ends by dedicating its good to all beings. Two explanations. One practice. In both schools, a good deed can end by being given away: the good isn't kept, it's sent out.
screen: `NO ONE CAN PURIFY ANOTHER.` · `THEY SHARE BY REJOICING.` · `GIVING IT AWAY GROWS IT.` · `TWO REASONS, ONE PRACTICE.` · then, large: `MAY IT BE SHARED.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open on your knees, palms up. Bring to mind five years of mornings, every sit, every kind word, every page you read. Then turn your palms over, and give all of it away, silently: to someone you love, to someone who has died, to someone you'll never meet, and then to every being, with no one kept out.
Dedication: giving away the good your practice has made, so others may share in it. In Pali, pattidana, the giving of a share.
Pocket this one: may it be shared, the good of today and of five years with it. Eleven days up the summit.

howItsDone: Buddhists may end chanting, a meditation, a gift or a memorial by dedicating its merit to others, often to departed relatives and to all beings; in Theravada communities others share by rejoicing (anumodana), often saying 'sadhu'.

fork.setup: your cousin says, 'karma is your own. dedicating merit is wishful thinking.' you want to give the best case for dedicating anyway, from inside the tradition. what do you say?
options: giving the good away is generosity, and whoever rejoices in it makes good of their own.
merit works like money: the temple can move it into anyone's account.
the Dhammapada says someone else can purify you if they try hard enough.
fork.reveal: both voices in the tradition agree on this much: rejoicing is a good act of one's own, and giving the good away is itself giving.

chat.meaning: Some Buddhists say the departed share by rejoicing (anumodana); others, that giving the good away is generosity that grows it. Both dedicate.

tie.story: King Bimbisara dedicated a meal to his departed relatives: may this be for our relatives; may they be happy.
tie.friend: Mai's mom is doing what the king did, and Mai can join the chanting knowing both reasons Buddhists give.

Tirokudda Sutta.meaning: a short text on the departed outside the walls

Bimbisara.meaning: king of Magadha, a lay follower of the Buddha

anumodana.meaning: rejoicing in someone else's good deed

Shantideva.meaning: a Mahayana teacher who wrote a guide to the bodhisattva's way

sources.ref: Khuddakapatha 7 (Tirokudda Sutta), also Petavatthu 1.5; the Bimbisara story from its commentary

sources.quoted: Purity and impurity belong to oneself, no one can purify another.

notes: Tirokudda Sutta (Khp 7 / Pv 1.5) paraphrased, including the dedication formula 'may this be for our relatives; may our relatives be happy' (idam vo natinam hotu, sukhita hontu natayo). The Bimbisara story (the meal, the wailing at night, the second dedicated gift) comes from the commentary and is labeled as such. Confirm.
Dhammapada 165 quoted from Max Müller 1881; confirm exact wording.

The Theravada account of merit-sharing through anumodana (rejoicing) and the Mahayana account of dedication (parinamana) as generosity are presented as two explanations held by Buddhists, ranking neither. Confirm the framing is fair to both.
Bodhicaryavatara 10: dedication for the sick, the frightened, beings in the hells and others; paraphrased. Confirm.
'Sadhu, sadhu' in Theravada temples is stated as 'you may hear'; confirm. Vietnamese chanting ending with a dedication (hoi huong) is attached to Mai's fictional family chùa. Confirm wording.
Original-language word: Pali pattidana (पत्तिदान); a Keeper may prefer Sanskrit parinamana for the Mahayana practice. Confirm spelling.
